newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Sporadic shooting as Zaire capital awaits rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sporadic shooting as Zaire capital awaits rebels.

text.p: Sporadic gunfire broke out in Zaire's capital on Saturday as it anxiously awaited Laurent Kabila's rebels after veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko left town and his ethnic guardsmen killed the army chief-of-staff.

Automatic weapons fire was heard in different parts of the city but it was unclear who was firing on whom. Witnesses reported a sustained small-arms firefight in a central market involving men in military uniform as well as civilian dress.

Kabila and a senior aide said that their forces had started to enter the usually bustling city of five million, where residents feared either a battle or an orgy of looting by bitter fleeing Mobutu loyalist soldiers.
There was no independent confirmation of their claim.
A correspondent with U.S.-based television network CNN reported no sign of the rebels on the road about 4 km (2.5 miles) from the airport.

"Our first column is entering the city and we expect to have the city under control by tonight. We want to move rapidly so that lawlessness does not get out of hand," Kabila's foreign affairs spokesman, Bizima Karaha, told Reuters by telephone from rebel headquarters in the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi.
Kabila told Reuters earlier that his forces were marching on the capital from the airport about 25 km (16 miles) away.
Karaha said Kabila would address the nation and make "an important announcement" later in the day.
The centre of Kinshasa, which spent a fourth night under military curfew, was largely deserted.
Residents in the direction of the airport remained indoors for safety and reported hearing shooting after dawn.
Unconfirmed reports said that residents in the opposition stronghold of Limite were turning out to welcome the rebels.

Karaha said that the rebels were "saddened" by the death of General Mahele Lieko Bokungu, defence minister and army chief-of-staff. A diplomat said Mahele had been due to meet Kabila in Zambia's capital Lusaka to discuss a transition of power.

A senior Western diplomat said Mahele was killed by Mobutu's Special Presidential Division at Camp Tshatshi, Mobutu's barracks residence. "He went to calm the guys down and then he was shot," the diplomat said.
Kabila said he had not heard of Mahele's death but termed it "very, very bad".

Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, left the capital for his northern jungle palace and stronghold on Friday. His emergency-rule government said Mobutu had left it in charge of national policy while keeping the title of president.
Now 66 and suffering from cancer, Mobutu is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
Mobutu, characteristically defiant, did not resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila and reportedly proposed by a peace plan formulated by South African President Nelson Mandela.
State television reported he had simply gone to his home region of Gbadolite on doctors' orders for "a few days of rest".

But news of his departure triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile. Diplomats said Morocco or France were likely destinations but CNN, citing a Mobutu spokesman, said that as of early Saturday he remained in Gbadolite.
Witnesses on Friday said the head of Mobutu's presidential guard, General Nzimbi Nzale, had fled with his family across the Zaire River to Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo.

Kabila, 56, and his rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis. They now control most of what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations, with a wealth of minerals and fertile farm land.
U.S., French, British, Belgian and Portuguese troops were on standby across the river in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
